Royal Raindrops is a distinctive ornamental crabapple with deeply cut, purple-red, finely serrated foliage unlike the broad, rounded leaves of most crabapple cultivars, opening with a heavy flush of magenta-pink spring flowers followed by small, persistent red fruit that hangs on into winter as forage for birds. It shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases — apple scab, fire blight, cedar-apple rust — that plague many older crabapple cultivars, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a small flowering shade tree. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; the small, hard fruit persists well into winter, providing months of ornamental and wildlife value beyond the spring bloom.

Spring Snow is prized for producing essentially no fruit at all, a genetic trait that makes it a popular choice where the messy fruit drop of ornamental crabapples is unwelcome — around patios, walkways, and driveways — while still delivering the classic crabapple spring show of dense, fragrant, pure white flowers covering the tree before the leaves fully emerge. Its clean, tidy habit and lack of fruit litter have made it one of the most widely planted flowering crabapples for urban and residential landscapes. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; watch for occasional fire blight and apple scab in humid climates.

Adams produces an abundant spring flush of deep rose-red buds opening to rose-pink flowers, followed by small, glossy, cherry-red fruit about half an inch across that persists into winter and draws robins, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. It is a reliably disease-resistant crabapple, showing good resistance to apple scab and cedar-apple rust that plague many older, less-improved cultivars, and its rounded, well-branched form makes it a dependable small flowering shade tree for a home landscape. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

Named for the noted Arnold Arboretum horticulturist, Donald Wyman produces a heavy spring flush of white flowers from pink buds, followed by small, bright red fruit that persists on the branches well into winter, often until the following spring, providing months of ornamental interest and emergency food for birds during lean winter weeks. It is a vigorous, wide-spreading, disease-resistant crabapple with good resistance to apple scab, making it a dependable, low-maintenance flowering shade tree. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches, giving it room to reach its considerable mature spread.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Red Jewel produces pure white spring flowers from pale pink buds, followed by an abundant crop of bright, glossy red, jewel-like fruit that holds on the branches into winter, providing striking color against bare branches and snow long after most ornamental trees have finished their season of interest. Its narrower, more upright-oval form than many crabapple cultivars fits smaller landscapes and tighter planting spots where a wide-spreading crabapple would not fit. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; shows good resistance to common crabapple diseases.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Sugar Tyme is a heavy, reliable bloomer, its deep pink buds opening to abundant, fragrant white flowers each spring, followed by a persistent crop of small, bright red fruit that holds through winter and draws birds when other food sources are scarce. It is one of the most disease-resistant crabapple cultivars available, showing strong resistance to apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew, which has made it a widely recommended low-maintenance choice by extension services across many regions. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Cloud 9 Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming Compact White Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, organically rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates; dogwoods are shallow-rooted and need consistent moisture, especially while establishing.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, siting it in morning sun with afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Cloud 9 is a compact, exceptionally heavy-flowering flowering dogwood selection, producing such a dense covering of large, pure white bracts each spring that the tree can appear almost solid white, an especially prolific bloom that has made it one of the most popular white dogwood cultivars in nursery production. Its smaller, more compact mature size than the species also suits it to smaller residential landscapes. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, since dogwoods are shallow-rooted and stressed by drought; prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering, and watch for powdery mildew and dogwood borer in humid climates.

common_name: Milky Way Kousa Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming White Kousa Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade; kousa dogwood is more sun-tolerant and disease-resistant than the native flowering dogwood.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Milky Way is an exceptionally floriferous kousa dogwood cultivar, its June flower display of creamy-white, pointed bracts so dense the branches appear covered in a blanket of white — a later bloom time than native flowering dogwood, extending the dogwood flowering season into early summer — followed in fall by raspberry-like red fruit that is edible and attracts wildlife, and by strong burgundy-red fall foliage color. As an Asian species, it is generally more resistant than native Cornus florida to the anthracnose and dogwood borer problems that trouble flowering dogwood in humid climates. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Wolf Eyes Kousa Dogwood (Variegated Dwarf Kousa Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; variegated foliage scorches in intense afternoon sun and benefits from some shade protection.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure that can scorch the variegated leaves. Wolf Eyes is a dwarf, slow-growing kousa dogwood grown as much for its striking foliage as its flowers, with leaves crisply edged in creamy white around a gray-green center, turning shades of pink and burgundy-red in fall, along with a modest early-summer flush of white bracts against the variegated backdrop. Its smaller mature size and dense, compact habit make it a strong specimen for smaller gardens or as a focal accent near a patio where the foliage can be appreciated up close. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

Cornus florida f. rubra is the classic pink-flowering form of the native flowering dogwood, its showy pink to rose-pink bracts opening in early spring before the leaves fully emerge, followed by clusters of glossy red fall fruit that draw songbirds and bright red-purple fall foliage. Seedlings grown from this form show a range of pink intensity, so gardeners wanting a guaranteed, consistent shade of pink should choose a named, vegetatively propagated cultivar rather than seed-grown stock. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, since dogwoods are shallow-rooted and stressed by drought; prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Blue Princess Holly (Meserve Hybrid Blue Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; plant a male pollinator such as 'Blue Prince' nearby, since Blue Princess is female and needs a compatible male to set berries.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant a compatible male pollinator such as 'Blue Prince' within about 30–40 feet, since this female cultivar needs cross-pollination to produce its signature berries. Blue Princess is one of the most widely planted Meserve hybrid hollies, its glossy, spiny, blue-green leaves and heavy crop of bright red winter berries combining the cold-hardiness of Ilex rugosa with the refined, lustrous foliage of English holly, making it more reliably cold-tolerant than English holly alone. Its dense, pyramidal, evergreen form works well as a specimen, foundation planting, or informal hedge, with the winter berry display providing strong seasonal interest and food for birds. Prune, if needed, in late winter before new spring growth begins.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade protection in the hottest climates. North Star was bred for reliable winter color retention and cold hardiness beyond that of most boxwood cultivars, holding a good, even green through winter without the bronzing that afflicts many boxwoods in cold or intense sun, while its dense, rounded, naturally compact habit needs relatively little shearing to maintain a tidy form. It is a good choice for formal hedging, edging, and foundation plantings where consistent winter appearance matters as much as summer form. Boxwoods need well-drained soil, since they are highly susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet sites; shear or hand-prune to shape in late winter or after the spring growth flush.
